a: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the simulation of human intelligence by machines, particularly computer systems. AI encompasses many subfields: machine learning (systems that learn from data), deep learning (multi-layered neural networks), natural language processing (understanding and generating language), computer vision (interpreting images), and robotics. AI is classified into three levels: Narrow AI (ANI — performs specific tasks, like facial recognition, language translation, chess engines; all current AI is narrow), General AI (AGI — matches human capabilities across all domains; not yet achieved), and Super AI (ASI — surpasses human intelligence; theoretical). Current AI uses techniques including supervised learning (trained on labeled data), unsupervised learning (finds patterns in unlabeled data), reinforcement learning (learns through trial and error with rewards), and transformer architectures (the 'T' in GPT, which revolutionized NLP). AI applications include virtual assistants, recommendation systems, self-driving cars, medical diagnosis, and scientific research. Major concerns include job displacement, bias in AI systems, privacy, and existential safety.

Blockchain is a distributed ledger technology that records transactions across many computers so that the record cannot be altered retroactively. Each 'block' contains a batch of transactions, a timestamp, and a cryptographic hash of the previous block, forming a chain. The technology was introduced in 2008 by an anonymous person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto as the underlying system for the cryptocurrency Bitcoin. Key features include decentralization (no single entity controls the network), transparency (all transactions are visible), immutability (once recorded, data cannot be changed without consensus), security (cryptographic hashing ensures integrity), and consensus mechanisms (Proof of Work — miners solve complex puzzles, Proof of Stake — validators stake tokens). Beyond cryptocurrencies, blockchain has applications in supply chain tracking, smart contracts (self-executing contracts on platforms like Ethereum), digital identity, voting systems, and NFTs. Challenges include scalability (transaction speed and energy use), regulation, and the environmental impact of Proof of Work mining.

a: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet ('the cloud'), rather than on local servers or personal devices. Key benefits include pay-as-you-go pricing, scalability, reliability, and reduced maintenance. The three main service models are: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS — virtual machines, storage, networking; AWS EC2, Google Compute Engine), Platform as a Service (PaaS — platforms for developing and deploying apps without managing underlying infrastructure; Google App Engine, Heroku), and Software as a Service (SaaS — fully managed applications accessible via browser; Gmail, Salesforce, Microsoft 365). Deployment models include public cloud (services shared across customers), private cloud (dedicated to one organization), hybrid cloud (combination), and multi-cloud (using multiple providers). Major cloud providers are Amazon Web Services (AWS, largest market share), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP). Cloud computing enables modern applications like streaming services, social media, data analytics, and AI training at global scale.

Nanotechnology involves manipulating matter at the nanoscale (1-100 nanometers, where 1 nm is one-billionth of a meter). At this scale, materials often exhibit unique properties different from their bulk behavior due to quantum effects and increased surface-area-to-volume ratio. Applications of nanotechnology include: medicine (targeted drug delivery, nanoparticles for cancer treatment, diagnostic imaging), electronics (smaller, faster transistors; quantum dots for displays; nanoscale memory), energy (more efficient solar cells, better batteries, hydrogen storage), materials science (stronger and lighter materials like carbon nanotubes and graphene, self-cleaning surfaces using the lotus effect), environmental (water purification membranes, pollution sensors), and consumer products (sunscreens with zinc oxide nanoparticles, stain-resistant fabrics, antimicrobial coatings). Richard Feynman first conceptualized nanotechnology in his 1959 talk 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom.' The field expanded dramatically after the invention of the scanning tunneling microscope (1981) and the discovery of fullerenes (1985) and carbon nanotubes (1991). Concerns include potential toxicity of nanoparticles, environmental impact, and ethical implications.

The Internet is a global network of interconnected computers that communicate using standardized protocols, primarily TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol). It was developed from ARPANET, a US Department of Defense project launched in 1969. Key inventors include Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn (TCP/IP protocols, 1974), Tim Berners-Lee (World Wide Web, 1989), and Marc Andreessen (first graphical web browser, Mosaic, 1993). The Internet works through a layered system: physical infrastructure (undersea cables, fiber optics, routers), IP addressing (unique identifiers for devices), DNS (Domain Name System, translating domain names to IP addresses), and application protocols (HTTP for web pages, SMTP for email, FTP for file transfer). Data travels in packets that are routed independently and reassembled at the destination. Key components include ISPs (Internet Service Providers), routers (direct traffic), servers (host content), and clients (user devices). The Internet has transformed communication, commerce, education, and entertainment. Major developments include the rise of social media, e-commerce, streaming services, cloud computing, and the Internet of Things (IoT).
